title: At the prompt or in a script
summary: The same bash for two jobs: habits that save keystrokes at the prompt become bugs in a script.

scheme: at the prompt   in a script
who reads  you, right now  nobody, later
names      the ones you    any: -rf, a b,
a failure  you see it      it goes on
goal       fast to type    right every time
text: The same bash, two jobs. At the prompt you type once, read the result and fix it on the spot. A script runs later, alone, on names and failures nobody planned for.
- Habits that save keystrokes at the prompt become bugs in a script. This lesson puts them side by side.
- ls prints names for your eyes. A name with a line break inside counts twice in ls | wc -l: fine to look around, wrong in a script.
- A script keeps the names themselves, in an array. nullglob makes a pattern that matches nothing give nothing, instead of itself.
- echo is fine for text you write yourself. Data can start with -n or -e, and echo takes it for an option.
- printf '%s\n' prints any value exactly as it is: the format comes first, the data after.
- At the prompt you see that cd worked. A script doesn't look: if cd fails, the next line runs in the folder you were in.
- So a script checks every step that matters, in the code: || exit 1 stops it right there.

scheme: prompt  $ rm *.tmp       you read the list
text: - A name can start with a dash, and a command would read it as options.
- -- says: no options after this point. ./ in front helps too: ./-rf.tmp doesn't start with a dash.
- Aliases, !! and history are prompt tools too: a script uses functions.
